The workflow here is the standard CoMFA and CoMSIA stack: dock or otherwise pose the ligands, calculate fields on a shared grid, fit them with partial least squares, and refuse the model if a scrambled label looks just as good. Xu and colleagues used that stack, together with docking and molecular dynamics, on thieno[3,2-b]pyrrole-5-carboxamide inhibitors of LSD1 [1]. The field settings below are the usual ones this kind of study is built from.

Put the potency on one scale

Collect IC50 values from assays you are willing to treat as comparable. Then convert to pIC50 before any fitting:

$$ \text{pIC}_{50} = -\log_{10}(\text{IC}_{50} \text{ in mol/L}) $$

The unit is the whole conversion. An IC50 of 1000 nM is \(10^{-6}\) mol/L, so the pIC50 is 6. The same number left in nanomolar and passed to a base-10 logarithm is a different, wrong, scale. Do this conversion once, and do not mix Ki or percent inhibition into the same column without saying so.

Hold out about 20 to 25 percent of the compounds as the external test set. The training set is the remaining 75 to 80 percent. The test compounds have to sit in the same chemical space as the training compounds. A test set that is a different series is an extrapolation, and a pretty \(r^2\) on it does not mean what it says.

Alignment is the model

CoMFA and CoMSIA descriptors exist on a grid in space. Two ligands contribute to the same grid point only if you have already decided how their atoms correspond. That decision is the alignment.

A common route is to take the protein structure from the Protein Data Bank, dock the series with a program such as SYBYL or AutoDock, and align every ligand to a reference pose. Redock a ligand whose experimental pose you know. An RMSD of 2.0 Å or less between the docked pose and that experimental pose is the usual acceptance check for this workflow. It is a check on the docking setup, not a guarantee that every other ligand found the right pose.

If the reference pose is wrong, every field shifts with it. The PLS model will still quote an \(r^2\). The contours will describe the error.

Fields

CoMFA

Comparative molecular field analysis uses two fields, steric and electrostatic.

  • Grid spacing: 2.0 Å.
  • Probe: an sp³ carbon with a charge of +1.
  • Energy cutoff: 30 kcal/mol, so a clash at one grid point cannot dominate the column.

CoMSIA

Comparative molecular similarity indices analysis adds hydrophobic, hydrogen-bond donor, and hydrogen-bond acceptor fields to the steric and electrostatic ones. The attenuation factor is 0.3. It sets how fast a field falls off with distance from the atoms. Changing it changes which grid points still see the ligand.

PLS, and the numbers it produces

Partial least squares is used because the grid columns are many, collinear, and noisy. Leave-one-out cross-validation on the training set chooses the optimal number of components (ONC) and produces \(q^2\), the cross-validated \(r^2\). That is an internal number. It is not the test set.

The model is then refit on the full training set with that component count. Report:

  • \(r^2\), the fit to the training compounds.
  • SEE, the standard error of that fit.
  • The F statistic for the regression.

A training \(r^2\) far above \(q^2\) is a model that has used components the left-out compounds do not support.

Tests the model is allowed to fail

Predict pIC50 for the compounds that were held out, and compute the external predictive \(r^2\), written \(r^2_\text{pred}\).

Tropsha’s diagnostics look at that external prediction more closely than a single \(r^2\). The set includes \(r^2_0\), the slopes \(k\) and \(k'\), \(r_m^2\), and \(\Delta r_m^2\). In this workflow a model is treated as predictive when \(k\) is near 1 and \(r_m^2\) is above 0.5. Those two cuts do not replace looking at the plot of predicted against measured pIC50.

Then scramble the biological activities, rebuild, and repeat. A real relationship collapses: the randomized trials should show low \(q^2\) and low \(r^2\). If they do not, the original fit was willing to explain noise.

Reading the contours

Only after those checks do the colors become a design suggestion.

Hydrophobic and hydrogen-bond contours, when you calculated CoMSIA fields, are read the same way: a color marks a region where that property, in this alignment, moved with potency.

The numbers, in one place

Metric What it is answering
\(q^2\) Did leave-one-out on the training set still predict?
\(r^2\) How well does the final model fit the training compounds?
\(r^2_\text{pred}\) How well does it predict the compounds you held out?
SEE How large are the training residuals?
F Is the regression distinguishable from no relationship?
\(r_m^2\), \(\Delta r_m^2\) Tropsha’s closer look at the external predictions
RMSD Did the docking setup reproduce a known pose?
Y-randomization Does the fit collapse when the labels are scrambled?

Bottom line

A 3D-QSAR study is not a hunt for a large \(r^2\). It is an aligned field model that has to predict a held-out set, fail when the labels are scrambled, and only then offer a contour as a place to change the molecule. The LSD1 paper is one worked example of that order [1]. The order is the part worth copying.

Reference

[1] Xu, Y., He, Z., Liu, H., Chen, Y., Gao, Y., Zhang, S., … and Yang, M. 3D-QSAR, molecular docking, and molecular dynamics simulation study of thieno[3,2-b]pyrrole-5-carboxamide derivatives as LSD1 inhibitors. RSC Advances, 2020, 10, 6927–6943.

item.title: Supervised vs. Unsupervised Methods in Machine Learning
item.description:
The split is not about which algorithm is fashionable. It is about whether each example already has an answer.

If the table carries a label, the task is supervised: learn the map from the other columns to that label. If it does not, the task is unsupervised: look for structure the table never names. People sometimes list a third family, reinforcement learning, where the signal is a reward collected over a sequence of actions. A static bioactivity table has no such loop. This note stays with the two tasks that table can actually support.

Read the row before you name the task

Take a chemical table with one molecule per line and columns such as molecule_chembl_id, smiles, standard_value, and class.

A row is one observation. The ChEMBL ID and the SMILES string identify that molecule. They are columns, but they are not ready-made features. A model needs numbers, and a SMILES string becomes numbers only after you compute descriptors or a fingerprint.

standard_value is already a number. If that number is what you are trying to predict, the task is regression. class is a category. In the labelling used on the acetylcholinesterase set, 1 means active and 0 means inactive. If that category is what you are trying to predict, the task is classification.

Calling every column a feature hides this. The features are the numeric columns you show the model. The label is the column you withhold. The identifier is neither.

Supervised learning

The model sees pairs: inputs, and the answer that went with them. After training, it assigns an answer to a row whose answer was hidden.

Two task types cover most bioactivity models.

  • Classification predicts a discrete label. Active or inactive, after you have defined those words with a cutoff, is classification.
  • Regression predicts a continuous value. Predicting the IC50 or the pIC50 itself, rather than a class derived from it, is regression.

The cutoff that created class is part of the supervised problem. Change the cutoff and you have changed the labels, even if every SMILES string stays the same.

Unsupervised learning

Here the model never sees an answer column. It can group rows, compress them, or estimate where the points sit densely. It cannot be “right” in the sense of matching a class you never provided.

Three techniques are the ones that show up on a chemical table.

  • Clustering groups points by similarity. On molecules, that is often a series of close analogs, or a point that sits in no series.
  • Dimensionality reduction draws a lower-dimensional map of the same rows. The map is a view of the representation you chose, not a photograph of chemical space.
  • Density estimation asks where the observations concentrate, which is also how isolated points become visible.

Association rules, known in retail as market-basket analysis, ask which items occur together in a basket. A single-molecule bioactivity table is not a basket. That method belongs to a different kind of data.

Evaluation is the uncomfortable part. With no held-out label, accuracy is the wrong word. What you can check is whether the grouping is stable under a second run or a second sample, and whether it lines up with a hypothesis you did not feed into the fit. Neither check turns the output into a supervised prediction.

Bottom line

Supervised learning requires a label on the training rows. Unsupervised learning starts without one. Classification and regression are the supervised pair. Clustering, projection, and density estimation are the unsupervised ones you will actually use on a compound table.

Choose the family from the table in front of you. If the answer column is missing, no change of algorithm will create it.

item.title: Chemical Databases Every ML Scientist Should Know for Drug Discovery
item.description:
The model is the last step. Before it, you have to decide which database actually holds the measurement you need.

Five public resources cover most of what a small-molecule project asks for. They are not substitutes. ChEMBL and BindingDB are bioactivity tables. PubChem is the broad assay archive. PDBbind pairs a bound structure with an affinity. BRENDA describes enzymes. Downloading the largest file is not the same as downloading the right one.

ChEMBL

is a manually curated set of bioactive molecules with drug-like properties, joined to the measurements reported for them. Those measurements include Ki, Kd, IC50, percent inhibition, and EC50.

That shape is what you want when the unit of analysis is “a molecule tested on a target.” Filtered well, the table becomes a screening set or a labelled file. A separate note walks through that curation for one target: search the protein, keep one activity type, collapse duplicate compounds, and only then assign a class. See .

The release notes are the place to read the current size. Quoting a compound count without saying whether it means unique structures or deposition records is how those two numbers get swapped.

BindingDB

is a public collection of measured binding affinities, mainly for proteins and small molecules. It also holds protein–protein, protein–peptide, and host–guest measurements.

A 2024 account of the database reported 2.9 million binding measurements spanning 1.3 million compounds and thousands of protein targets [1]. The first version of this note, written in 2022, described a smaller collection: more than 1.2 million measurements, more than 6,400 protein targets, and about 550,000 small molecules. Both figures are snapshots. The live site is the one to quote for a paper.

The practical entry points are searches, prepared datasets, and a similarity screen that takes an external compound set and looks for related bioactivity already in the database. Downloads have included SD files, TSV, and a database dump. Programmatic access has included a REST API, structured URLs, and KNIME. Menus move. The distinction that does not move is the content: affinities, with the target and the ligand identified.

Find My Compound’s Target

This tool takes a query molecule, finds similar compounds already in BindingDB, and returns the targets of those neighbors when they pass a similarity cutoff and an affinity cutoff. It is a neighbor search. It is not a model trained to predict a new mechanism, and a target that appears in the result is only as reliable as the neighbor and the cutoff you set.

Find Compounds for My Target

The companion search goes the other way. You name a target and ask which compounds have measurements against it. The curated rows draw on BindingDB itself and on outside sources, including ChEMBL, PubChem BioAssay, and D3R. Read the source of each row. A Ki from one database and an IC50 imported from another are not the same label.

PubChem

, at the National Center for Biotechnology Information, is the broad public archive. For a given substance it can hold chemical identity together with biochemical, pharmacological, toxicological, and other deposited description. It is free to search.

PubChem BioAssay stores the experimental records: small-molecule screens and RNAi experiments, each tied to the depositor who submitted it. Every tested substance is given an activity outcome, commonly active, inactive, or inconclusive. The depositor assigns that outcome from the assay. PubChem does not impose one potency cutoff on every record. A reported IC50, EC50, or Ki can sit beside the flag. The flag does not replace the protocol.

You can query by name, by SMILES, or by a structure you draw, and ask for an exact compound, a similar one, or a substructure. The assay page is where you go when two values disagree: the record includes the experiment, not only the number. PubChem also groups assays by protein or gene target, by assay type, by project, and by relationships such as shared active compounds.

PubChemPy

is the Python client. It covers lookup by name, substructure, and similarity, plus standardization, format conversion, depiction, and property retrieval. Use it when the next step is a table in a notebook rather than a page in the browser.

PDBbind

collects experimentally measured Kd, Ki, and IC50 values for complexes that are already in the Protein Data Bank. The useful object is the pair. A structure without an affinity, or an affinity without the complex it was measured on, answers a different question.

Basic information on each complex has been open to browse. Downloading the full contents, and some of the site’s tools, has required a free registration under a license agreement, for both academic and industrial users. Access to this resource has changed more than once since this note was first written. Check the current terms before you build a pipeline on a bulk file.

BRENDA

is an enzyme information system compiled from the primary literature. The name comes from its start in Braunschweig. It was developed for years at the University of Cologne and remains a public enzyme resource, not a compound-screening warehouse.

An entry is organized around the enzyme. It covers classification and nomenclature, the reaction and its specificity, functional and kinetic parameters, structure and stability, how the enzyme was isolated or prepared, the literature those facts came from, and cross-references to sequence or three-dimensional structure. You search it by EC number, enzyme name, organism, or a combination of those.

Academic and other non-commercial use is free. Commercial use requires a license. The project site states the current terms. BRENDA is the wrong download if the goal is a matrix of drug-like molecules and their IC50 values. It is the right one if the question is what the enzyme does and under which conditions.

Which one to open first

Ask what a row in the training file is supposed to mean.

  • A molecule tested on a target, with Ki, IC50, or a related potency: ChEMBL, then curate.
  • A binding affinity as the object of interest: BindingDB.
  • The original assay, including who decided “active”: PubChem BioAssay.
  • A 3D complex that must stay attached to its affinity: PDBbind.
  • The enzyme’s reaction, specificity, and kinetics: BRENDA.

ChEMBL, BindingDB, and PubChem can be pulled into a script. PDBbind and BRENDA are still databases you read carefully before you model anything derived from them. The script does not fix a file that answered a different question.

Reference

[1] Liu, T. et al. BindingDB in 2024: a FAIR knowledgebase of protein-small molecule binding data. Nucleic Acids Research, 2025, 53, D1633–D1644.

item.title: How to Perform Data Curation and Classify Bioactivity Data on ChEMBL Database
item.description:
A classifier does not learn activity. It learns the labels you attached to the molecules.

ChEMBL will give you the measurements. It will not give you the labels. For one target the download has many rows, often several for the same compound, some with no number, and a continuous IC50 that is not yet a class. This note turns the human acetylcholinesterase table into a file a classifier can train on: one row per molecule, a mean potency, and a class that leaves the uncertain middle out.

What the download actually contains

ChEMBL is a curated collection of bioactive, drug-like molecules and the measurements reported for them. Two counts on the release notes are easy to mix up. Compound records count depositions. Unique compounds are fewer, because the same structure can arrive from more than one source.

The ChEMBL 30 release, prepared on 22 February 2022, contained 2,786,911 compound records, 2,157,379 compounds, 1,458,215 assays, and 14,855 targets [1]. ChEMBL 33, prepared on 31 May 2023, contained 3,051,613 compound records, 2,399,743 compounds, 1,610,596 assays, and 15,398 targets [2]. A later paper describes the same platform and the kinds of data it holds [3]. Use the current release notes if you need today’s size. The curation steps below do not depend on it.

One target, one activity type

Search the target name, not a disease and not a compound, when the model is meant to describe that protein. Acetylcholinesterase returns many targets. The one used here is the human protein, CHEMBL220. Pick the organism on purpose. A homolog is a different label.

On the target report, the activity chart shows how those measurements were reported. In the interface used for this tutorial, IC50 was the common type, listed 8,205 times. That count grows as new papers are added. Treat it as a snapshot of the download, not as a property of the enzyme.

Download the IC50 slice as CSV or TSV. Then keep four columns, and delete the rest before you open the file in a notebook:

  • Molecule ChEMBL ID
  • Smiles
  • Standard Type
  • Standard Value

ChEMBL standard IC50 values are in nanomolar. If a later export renames a column, rename it back to this list. The notebook expects these headers, and it expects Standard Value to be a number.

One row per molecule

The same ChEMBL ID often appears more than once. Laboratories did not run the same assay. The values disagree, and both rows are “the” measurement until you decide on a rule.

The rule in this tutorial is a mean of Standard Value on the linear nanomolar scale, grouped by ChEMBL ID. That is a teaching choice. A factor of ten in potency is not symmetric on a linear scale, and a mean mixes assays that were not run under the same conditions. It is enough to build a labelled practice set. It is not assay-aware curation.

After the mean is attached, keep the first row for each ID and drop rows that still have a missing value. Averaging first matters: the mean has to see every replicate before the extras are deleted.

import pandas as pd

columns = ["Molecule ChEMBL ID", "Smiles", "Standard Type", "Standard Value"]
x = pd.read_csv("ache.csv")
x = x[columns]
x["Standard Value"] = pd.to_numeric(x["Standard Value"], errors="coerce")

x["mean_value"] = x.groupby("Molecule ChEMBL ID")["Standard Value"].transform("mean")
x = x.drop_duplicates("Molecule ChEMBL ID", keep="first")
x = x.dropna()

to_numeric(..., errors="coerce") turns anything that is not a number into a missing value, so a footnote or a blank cell cannot silently become text and break the mean. Restricting the frame to the four columns first stops dropna from rejecting a molecule because some unused field was empty.

The class is a gap, not a line

Potent enzyme inhibitors in this literature often sit in the nanomolar range. For a classification exercise, call a molecule active when its mean IC50 is at most 1000 nM, which is 1 µM. Call it inactive when the mean is above 10000 nM, which is 10 µM. Everything between those two cuts is left out of the file.

active = x.loc[x["mean_value"] <= 1000].copy()
inactive = x.loc[x["mean_value"] > 10000].copy()
active["Class"] = 1
inactive["Class"] = 0

combined = pd.concat([active, inactive], axis=0)
combined.to_csv("ache_labelled.csv", index=False)

.copy() matters. Assigning Class on a sliced frame is how pandas loses the new column or warns that it might. The saved file contains only the two tails. It is smaller than the curated table, and it is enriched for molecules whose mean fell clearly on one side.

What this file is

The CSV is a practice set for one target and one endpoint. A few limits travel with it.

  • The class is a cutoff on a mean, not a second experiment.
  • Replicates were averaged on a linear scale, across assays that were not matched.
  • Molecules between 1 µM and 10 µM are absent, so a model never has to make the close call.
  • The same cuts on a different target, or on Ki rather than IC50, would be a different labelling decision. Do that in a separate file.

Those choices are the model, as much as the classifier you train afterwards.

References

[1] ChEMBL 30 release note, 10 March 2022. Data prepared 22 February 2022.

[2] ChEMBL 33 release note, 13 June 2023. Data prepared 31 May 2023.

[3] Zdrazil, B. et al. The ChEMBL Database in 2023: a drug discovery platform spanning multiple bioactivity data types and time periods. Nucleic Acids Research, 2024, 52, D1180–D1192.
